definition: Delineate means to describe or set out something in precise detail.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word delineate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know delineate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The pastry syllabus delineates each skill to be mastered, week by week, down to the fold count for a proper croissant.
Mention is far milder than delineate — a mention is a wave of the hand, the subject raised and passed by, while to delineate is to set the thing out in exact detail.
Describe goes further than mention — shape and color arrive; delineate claims the most: every line drawn, every edge exact, nothing left to guess.

Itemize means to break a whole into a list, piece by piece — an invoice itemizes its charges. Delineate does more than list: it draws the boundary lines, fixing exactly where one duty or region ends and the next begins.

Map out is the loose planning phrase — you map out a road trip or a semester on the back of an envelope. Delineate is its buttoned-up cousin: the same ground covered, but in precise detail that can survive an argument.

It names which cousin takes the orchard rows east of the ditch, who gets the beehives and who the extractor, what happens to the tractor if two heirs want it, and the order in which the paintings choose their owners.
The lawyer had warned her that loose wording breeds feuds; ten years on, the cousins still gather for the harvest, and nobody has ever gone to court.
Delineate is the exact word for what that will does, because it means to describe or set out something in precise detail — to draw the lines so plainly that nothing is left to argue about.
Describe would cover a loose sketch; delineate promises edges.
Delineate is for briefings and paperwork that must survive argument: duties, boundaries, ground rules.
When plain telling will do, describe; when you only need the gist, sketch.

When the community garden doubled in size, the old handshake agreements stopped working.
Two families planted the same corner bed in the same week, and the compost turns nobody had promised to do went undone.
So the board spent a winter drafting a charter that delineates everything: each plot's borders are drawn to the inch, and every shared chore is assigned to a named member for a named month.
A few gardeners grumbled that the document read like a treaty.
The next spring there was not a single dispute over ground, and the compost got turned on schedule.
